object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triaged event representing something that broke, tracked through its lifecycle.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A signal from the monitoring platform (or manually raised) indicating a possible problem; can originate an incident.

source_references.excerpt: And an alert -- identified how? / Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket that can indicate an incident.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: A rating of blast radius and technical impact of an incident, from SEV1 (most severe) to SEV4 (least).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: A rating of customer urgency for an incident, from P1 to P4, independent of severity.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.
Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: Incident State
object_types.definition: The lifecycle status of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can serve as incident commander (a named person for the duration of the incident).

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A group that owns a service on a standing basis.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system/service that can be affected by an incident and is owned by exactly one team.

source_references.excerpt: How is a service identified? / Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

fact_types.name: Incident is based on Alert
readings: Alert is the basis for Incident

source_references.excerpt: If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.
So an incident has an alert, or a customer report, or both, and never neither. / Never neither. The declare form won't let you.

fact_types.name: Incident is based on Ticket
readings: Ticket is the basis for Incident

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us. ... the alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes.
So an incident has an alert, or a customer report, or both, and never neither.

fact_types.name: Incident has Severity
readings: Severity is the severity of Incident

source_references.excerpt: Every declared incident has a severity. That's mandatory, you can't declare without one.
The incident record carries the current severity.

fact_types.name: Incident has Priority
readings: Priority is the priority of Incident

source_references.excerpt: Priority too. Support sets it, and it's on every incident.

fact_types.name: Incident is in State
readings: Incident State is the state of Incident

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed. ... Exactly one at a time.
The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.
Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.
A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.
And an incident affects a service? / One or more. Usually one, sometimes several when it's an infrastructure thing.

source_references.excerpt: Incident B is a duplicate of incident A.

inferred_constraints.fact_type: Incident is a duplicate of Incident
inferred_constraints.description: Chains of duplicates (C dup of B, B dup of A) should not form; everything should point directly at the primary. Stated as intended rule but not enforced by the system.

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? ... It's wrong. If C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point at A. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

We had a SEV1 at four in the morning on a Sunday where the affected surface was the marketing site. Everything down, nobody awake, no revenue impact. That was a P4.

ambiguities.description: The term 'sev' is colloquially used by staff to refer to either Severity or Priority interchangeably, causing real operational confusion, even though the model treats them as distinct, independent attributes.

source_references.excerpt: And people say "sev" when they mean either. Somebody says "we've got a sev one" in a channel and I don't know whether to page the whole platform team or ring one account manager.

ambiguities.description: The term 'owner' is ambiguous between two distinct concepts: the Incident Commander (a temporary role for the duration of an incident) and the Service Owner (a standing team assignment). The transcript flags this as a recurring real-world collision, though the model resolves it into two separate fact types.

source_references.excerpt: Nadia, you said commander is a role, not a job title. Is there a different sense of owner? ... And in a channel, "who owns this?" means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: Owen claims 'a P1 is always a SEV1' but this is refuted by Nadia with concrete counterexamples; the transcript explicitly states no correlation/subset constraint should be modeled between Severity and Priority values, despite the intuitive belief some staff hold.

source_references.excerpt: A P1 is always a SEV1. / That is not true. ... Halberd Financial goes down ... That's a P1 all day. It's a SEV3.

ambiguities.description: An informal 'monitoring' status is used by staff between mitigated and resolved, but explicitly rejected as a formal state since it is not in the system's dropdown. This is a clear instance of terminology used informally that does not map to a modeled value.

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. / That's not a state, that's a thing people write in the channel. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: The duplicate-of relationship's acyclic/no-chaining rule is described as the intended rule but explicitly NOT enforced by the system today ('two-deep' chains have been observed), raising the question of whether this constraint should be modeled as a hard rule or just documented as an aspiration.

source_references.excerpt: It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Whether incidents later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is is explicitly left undecided and deferred to another stakeholder (Ravi); no 'cause classification' concept exists in the current model despite extensive discussion, and this represents a known gap/future extension.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a decision here today? / No, and it's above all three of us. ... Parking it explicitly, then. Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Nadia states incidents are never deleted ('we never delete incidents'), flagged as relevant later, connecting to the duplicate-handling discussion where duplicate incidents are also not deleted but linked instead -- suggesting an implicit business rule against deletion, though it's never formalized as a hard constraint in the read-back.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.
And you can't just delete two of them, because people are already working in them and the timelines have real content.

ambiguities.description: It is unclear whether the 'manual alert' created when an engineer manually notices and raises something is modeled identically to a monitoring-platform-generated alert (same Alert entity/identifier scheme), or whether it constitutes a distinct subtype needing its own identification/source attribute.

source_references.excerpt: If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

ambiguities.description: The final exchange (Kit having already left the call but leaving audio on) is a humorous edge case about presence/connectivity, not a modeling fact, but underscores that Kit's contributions (duplicates, the never-delete/classification issue) were delivered somewhat informally/remotely, raising a soft question about the authority/reliability of his input on unresolved items.

source_references.excerpt: Then I've got what I need, and Kit can go back to his offsite. / I've been back at the offsite for ten minutes, I just left this on.
